packs.title: Historic rooms, city streets and park views
packs.promise: Read historic places, test water and make from the city’s actual paths and facades.

q.s: Write from the season that is actually here.
st: Choose three permitted path positions in the Formal Gardens, keeping all plant beds and fountains untouched.
At the first, notice a line or edge. At the second, choose a texture that is visible from the path. At the third, listen for a sound without needing birds or particular weather.
Write three original sentences, each using one of your observations. Let the sentences move from an outward view to a smaller detail; do not borrow plant labels as your own poetry.
Read the sentences quietly to yourself and revise one word so it describes today’s actual garden. Add the season and one thing you did not assume, such as a flower being in bloom.

q.s: Test one visible change at a time.
st: Enter the opened Wonders of Water exhibit and choose a water-channel activity that current directions permit visitors to manipulate.
Make a first observation, then change one available control or arrangement as instructed. Record what you changed and what actually happened to the water, without guessing a hidden mechanism.
Repeat with two more permitted changes. Reset between trials where instructed and leave room for other visitors. If you could not keep other conditions the same, record that limitation.
Write three “change → observation” records and one cautious comparison. Distinguish a result you saw from an explanation you would need another test to support.

q.s: Walk to one actual viewpoint and bring its scale back.
st: Find the opened parking-side path and current park directions to the northern quarry overlook. Check barriers before committing to the return route.
Walk the designated path at your own pace. On the way, notice one transition from parking-area surroundings to the quarry-edge view without leaving the path.
At the permitted overlook, choose two features that help you read the quarry’s scale, such as the relationship between the cliff rim and water. Stay behind every barrier.

Return along the same opened path, then write the outward transition, your two scale observations and one thing the return view changed. Record your own elapsed time if useful; the plan’s ten minutes is an estimate.

packs.title: Downtown arts and Innovation Quarter afternoons
packs.promise: Follow books, gallery rooms, public art and reused buildings across two connected afternoons.

q.s: Collect the sources that let a place tell different stories.
st: Find the opened North Carolina Collection through current library directions. Choose three readable records about Winston-Salem or its local history, using different items or source types.
For each, note the title, author or responsible organization, date if stated and the form of the item. An absent date stays “not stated”; do not supply one.
Read a brief permitted part of each and write one city-specific topic it can help investigate. Keep your records paraphrased rather than copying long passages or private archival documents.
Arrange the three records into a small reading path: begin with one topic and explain why the second and third would add a different kind of evidence. Leave all materials as directed.

q.s: Give one vertical facade a small new frame.
st: Choose a lawful public Fourth Street view that keeps the facade visible without standing in traffic or blocking a doorway.
Notice one repeated opening pattern, one detail near the base and one part of the building’s vertical outline. Keep your descriptions tied to what you can see.
Draw a small original postcard crop that brings those three details together. You can also write a framing description if drawing is uncomfortable.
Write your own two-sentence caption using a present-day observation. Put any historical fact in a separate note with the City source, and keep residential spaces out of your imagined scene.

q.s: Collect the lines that join an outdoor art space.
st: Find an opened public route into the art park, keeping events and maintenance barriers outside your activity.
Collect three different visible relationships: a ground line leading into the park, towers arranged in the space, and the bandstand or currently visible mural wall.
For each, write where one form points, repeats or meets another. Do not require mist, read an unreadable artist credit as fact or assume today’s mural matches an older photograph.
Draw a small relationship map using your three observations. Add one sentence explaining how the entry line changes your first view of the space.
